newsitem.title: USA: Major league sports quietly oppose Moynihan bill.
newsitem.headline: Major league sports quietly oppose Moynihan bill.

text.p: U.S. Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan's controversial bill to curb tax exempt financing for professional sports stadiums is running up against a powerful opponent -- major league sports associations working quietly behind the scenes to kill it.

While state and local government groups have conducted splashy letter writing campaigns urgently requesting Moynihan and key House and Senate finance panel chairmen to rethink any bill, lobbyists for major league baseball, football and basketball are routinely showing up at monthly group strategy sessions and weighing in with telephone calls to Capitol Hill on the issue, one lobbyist said.

"The fact that think much of Moynihan's bill is not new news to any" said William Cable, vice president of Timmo Co, outside lobbyists for Major League Baseball, which oversees the interests of top sports teams.
But "we have no intention of becoming very visible" on the issue, Cable said in a telephone interview with Reuters. "It's not about us. It's about local authority and autonomy."
Cable said he attended several monthly meetings organized by the U.S. Conference of Mayors to monitor the legislation.
"I've been to several meetings and there have been others from baseball (as well as ) almost all of the other team sports as well," he said.
"I don't think there's been any written correspondence" by sports groups, he added. "There have been a lot of conversations, but I don't think there's anything on paper.
Cable said his group opposes Moynihan's bill, which opponents say will make public stadium financing almost impossible, because it encroaches on local decisionmaking.

"These are decisions best made by local policymakers," Cable said. "Cities and counties know their business at least as well as a senator from 1,000 miles away. They are the right ones to make the decisions."
Moynihan shook the municipal bond market in June 1995 when he introduced a bill to bar use of tax exempt bonds for professional sports stadiums and gave it an immediate effective date.
Following heavy opposition, he agreed in late 1996 to change the effective date to the date of first committee action, which would not have been before April 1 this year.
Moynihan in March again agreed to delay the bill's effective date to the day that any bill is signed by the President.
No committee action has been scheduled on the bill to date, but lobbyistMoynihan stadiums measure could get folded into broad tax legislation that Capitol Hill takes up later this year.
A spokesperson for the National Footbal League Players Association was not available for comment.
